prompt: What IR absorption does the O–H bond of a carboxyl group give?

choices.text: A very broad absorption over 2500 to 3300 cm^−1
An intense absorption near 2250 cm^−1
choices.why: That is the C≡N absorption of a saturated nitrile.

choices.text: An absorption between 1710 and 1760 cm^−1
choices.why: That range is the carboxyl C=O absorption.

choices.text: No absorption, because the hydrogen is acidic
choices.why: The carboxyl O–H gives one of the two characteristic absorptions of a –CO2H group.

explanation: Carboxylic acids have two characteristic IR absorptions: a very broad O–H absorption over 2500 to 3300 cm^−1 and a C=O absorption between 1710 and 1760 cm^−1.

prompt: Most carboxylic acid samples contain hydrogen-bonded (dimeric) carboxyl groups. Near what wavenumber is their C=O absorption centered, in cm^−1?
explanation: Free (monomeric) carboxyl groups absorb at 1760 cm^−1, but the more commonly encountered dimeric carboxyl groups absorb in a broad band centered around 1710 cm^−1, as in butanoic acid (Figure 20.8.1).

prompt: How does conjugation with an alkene or benzene ring affect the C=O stretching absorption of a carboxylic acid?

choices.text: It lowers the frequency by 20 to 30 cm^−1
It raises the frequency by 20 to 30 cm^−1
choices.why: As with other carbonyl groups, conjugation lowers the C=O frequency.

choices.text: It lowers the frequency by about 50 cm^−1
choices.why: 50 cm^−1 is the gap between free (1760 cm^−1) and dimeric (1710 cm^−1) carboxyl groups. Conjugation lowers the frequency by 20 to 30 cm^−1.

choices.text: It has no effect on the C=O absorption
choices.why: Conjugation lowers the C=O frequency, as it does for other carbonyl-containing functional groups.

explanation: As with other carbonyl-containing functional groups, conjugation with an alkene or benzene ring lowers the frequency of the C=O stretch by 20 to 30 cm^−1.

prompt: Near what wavenumber does the C≡N bond of an aromatic nitrile such as benzonitrile absorb in the IR, in cm^−1?
explanation: Nitriles show an intense C≡N absorption near 2250 cm^−1 for saturated compounds and 2230 cm^−1 for aromatic and conjugated molecules. Few other functional groups absorb in this region, so IR is highly diagnostic for nitriles.

prompt: Cyclopentanecarboxylic acid and 4-hydroxycyclohexanone are both C6H10O2, and both contain an –OH and a C=O group. Which IR feature identifies the carboxylic acid?

choices.text: A very broad –OH absorption over 2500 to 3300 cm^−1
An intense C≡N absorption near 2250 cm^−1
choices.why: Neither compound is a nitrile.

choices.text: Any absorption in the C=O stretching region
choices.why: Both compounds have a C=O group, so a C=O band alone can't tell them apart.

choices.text: Any absorption showing that an O–H bond is present
choices.why: Both compounds have an –OH group. What marks the acid is the very broad carboxyl O–H band spanning 2500 to 3300 cm^−1.

explanation: Both isomers have –OH and C=O groups, but only the carboxylic acid shows the very broad carboxyl O–H absorption over 2500 to 3300 cm^−1 (Exercise 20.8.1).

prompt: Carboxyl carbons absorb from 165 to 185 δ in the ^13C NMR spectrum. Which acid's carboxyl carbon would you expect to absorb nearest 185 δ?

choices.text: Butanoic acid, CH3CH2CH2CO2H
Benzoic acid, C6H5CO2H
choices.why: Aromatic acids absorb near the upfield end of the range, about 165 δ.

choices.text: Acrylic acid, H2C=CHCO2H
choices.why: α,β-Unsaturated acids absorb near the upfield end of the range, about 165 δ.

choices.text: p-Nitrobenzoic acid, p-O2NC6H4CO2H
choices.why: This is an aromatic acid, so it absorbs near the upfield end of the range, about 165 δ.

explanation: Aromatic and α,β-unsaturated acids absorb near the upfield end of the 165 to 185 δ range (about 165 δ), and saturated aliphatic acids near the downfield end (about 185 δ). Butanoic acid is the only saturated aliphatic acid here.

prompt: In what range do nitrile carbons absorb in the ^13C NMR spectrum?

choices.why: That is the range for carboxyl carbons.

choices.text: Near 210 δ
choices.why: A ketone C=O carbon, as in 4-hydroxycyclohexanone, absorbs near 210 δ.

choices.text: Near 12 δ
choices.why: 12 δ is where the –CO2H proton absorbs in the ^1H NMR spectrum.

explanation: Nitrile carbons absorb in the range 115 to 130 δ, upfield of carboxyl carbons (165 to 185 δ).

prompt: Near what chemical shift, in δ, does the acidic –CO2H proton normally absorb in the ^1H NMR spectrum?
explanation: The –CO2H proton normally absorbs as a singlet near 12 δ; in the spectrum of phenylacetic acid it appears at 12.0 δ. Its exact position depends on concentration and solvent, which change the extent of hydrogen-bonding.

prompt: What happens to the –CO2H absorption in the ^1H NMR spectrum when D2O is added to the sample tube?

choices.text: It disappears, as deuterium replaces the –CO2H proton
It shifts upfield to about 4 δ, near H–C–O protons
choices.why: 4 δ is near where an H–C–O proton absorbs. Exchange with D2O removes the –CO2H signal instead.

choices.text: It doubles in intensity as deuterium adds a signal
choices.why: Replacing the proton with deuterium removes the signal from the ^1H spectrum; it doesn't strengthen it.

choices.text: It splits into a doublet from coupling to deuterium
choices.why: Exchange with D2O replaces the proton by deuterium, so the signal disappears rather than splitting.

explanation: As with alcohols, the –CO2H proton can be replaced by deuterium when D2O is added to the sample tube, causing the absorption to disappear from the ^1H NMR spectrum.

prompt: A C6H10O2 compound, either cyclopentanecarboxylic acid or 4-hydroxycyclohexanone, shows a ^1H NMR absorption near 12 δ and a ^13C NMR absorption near 170 δ. Which compound is it?

choices.text: Cyclopentanecarboxylic acid, since both peaks fit a –CO2H group
4-Hydroxycyclohexanone, since the 12 δ peak fits its –OH proton
choices.why: 4-Hydroxycyclohexanone would show an H–C–O absorption near 4 δ. A singlet near 12 δ is typical of a –CO2H proton.

choices.text: 4-Hydroxycyclohexanone, since the 170 δ peak fits its ketone carbon
choices.why: The ketone C=O carbon of 4-hydroxycyclohexanone absorbs near 210 δ. 170 δ falls in the carboxyl range, 165 to 185 δ.

choices.text: Either one, since these two isomers give the same NMR spectra
choices.why: The isomers have different functional groups and give clearly different absorptions.

explanation: Cyclopentanecarboxylic acid shows its –CO2H proton near 12 δ and its –CO2H carbon near 170 δ. 4-Hydroxycyclohexanone would instead show an H–C–O absorption near 4 δ in the ^1H spectrum and a C=O absorption near 210 δ in the ^13C spectrum (Exercise 20.8.2).
